[{:db/id 17592186124592 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a024553e-c27e-5c68-a828-a6ec8223e683"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124403 :question/problem "Consider the vector space $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $\mathbb R$ with degrees at most $2.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\big\{ 0,t^2 \big\}$ is a linearly independent set in $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$

II. $-5t^2$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\big\{ 0, t^2 \big\}$

III. $\big\{ 0, t^2 \big\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124489 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ac0d302b-9680-52bd-b447-e8dfc12a3304"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124302 :question/problem "Consider the vector space $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ of all $2 \times 2$ matrices over $\mathbb{R}.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. ![](images/e9/e98eb00ac7ee6ffb83d4a902d92e9bda4434e6bfaeae1fb91a210849d3e1991f.svg) is a linearly independent set in $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$

II. $[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ![](images/71/716877f60112610eae19b094ca691edf0c0d2ecdffc54dc0b785d66c96e64909.svg)

III. ![](images/cc/ccd021603e72ceb60be92eabec243bfdd5ce33eb22a6b801030a05efc02a861d.svg) is a basis of $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation
![](images/a1/a16ee652347a67e66994875711dff835418bfcfb4f85a058a80f9164af525cab.svg)
is true if and only if $x_1=x_2=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,
![](images/f1/f173928232bbfd7680c2952250c78e7ba354bd4851cb4783bd531cc683044db5.svg)

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of 
![](images/74/7449707a6aa218f65cc22db3a56e8ed9391e3b5e562301e77fd62cb2f3dad20a.svg)
since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry $a_{11} = 0\mathbin{:}$
![](images/b9/b952b253393b4d14572b41ad1ca265e3b858edeec36e4c937f644621ae497294.svg)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124490 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2dd6c5c5-53ed-575f-8c9f-dc822f51b9e6" "question-c626f6f5-d2a8-58e2-a687-8abd5e7a0913"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124303 :question/problem "Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}$ is a basis of $V$

II. $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}$ spans $V$

III. $\left\{  -\mathbf{b_2}, 3\mathbf{b_1}\right\}$ is linearly dependent" :question/worked-solution "Since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $\mathcal{B}$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $\mathcal{B}$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{2}+{x}_{2}(-{b}_{1})+{x}_{3}({b}_{3}+{b}_{1}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{2}+({x}_{3}-{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly independent, gives
![](images/62/625e812c25818cec68c6a5bcd59a39945feb09526607244e42059ed8af6f9b08.svg)
Also, $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3\mathbf{b}_3
=
x_2\mathbf{b}_2+(x_3-x_1)(-\mathbf{b}_1)+x_3 (\mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1})
$$

- Statement II is false. In order for $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}$ to span $V,$ every element of $\mathcal{B}$ must be able to be expressed as a linear combination of elements of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}.$ But the vector $\mathbf{b}_1 \in \mathcal{B}$ can't be written as a linear combination of the elements of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}.$

- Statement III is false. If $\left\{  -\mathbf{b_2}, 3\mathbf{b_1}\right\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist $x_1$ and $x_2$ not both zero such that

$$
x_1(-\mathbf{b_2}) + x_2(3\mathbf{b_1}) = \mathbf{0}.
$$

Then, we would have

$$
(3x_2) \cdot \mathbf{b_1} + (-x_1) \cdot \mathbf{b_2} + 0 \cdot \mathbf{b}_3= \mathbf{0}.
$$

But this would mean that $\mathcal{B} = \left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly dependent, which contradicts the fact that $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis of $V.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186360516 :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{3}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $3.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{0,{t}^{3}\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${R}_{3}[t]$

II. $-{t}^{3}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{0,{t}^{3}\}$

III. $\{0,{t}^{3}\}$ is a basis of ${R}_{3}[t]$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186360514 :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{3}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $3.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{0,t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${R}_{3}[t]$

II. $3{t}^{2}-t$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{0,t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}\}$

III. $\{0,t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}\}$ is a basis of ${R}_{3}[t]$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186360513 :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{2}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $2.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{t,{t}^{2}\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${R}_{2}[t]$

II. ${t}^{2}+1$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{t,{t}^{2}\}$

III. $\{t,{t}^{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}_{2}[t]$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation 

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot t+{x}_{2}\cdot {t}^{2}=0,
$$

 
is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is false. Notice that all linear combinations of

$$
\{t,{t}^{2}\}
$$

result in polynomials without the constant term.

- Statement III is false. Indeed, the polynomial ${t}^{2}+1$ can't be written as a linear combination of the set  $\{t,{t}^{2}\}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-a024553e-c27e-5c68-a828-a6ec8223e683" :question/id #uuid "a024553e-c27e-5c68-a828-a6ec8223e683" :question/math-academy-id "q-107130" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{2}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $2.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{2,{t}^{2}\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${R}_{2}[t]$

II. $2+{t}^{2}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{2,{t}^{2}\}$

III. $\{2,{t}^{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}_{2}[t]$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation 

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot 2+{x}_{2}\cdot {t}^{2}=0,
$$

 
is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
2+{t}^{2}=1\cdot 2+1\cdot {t}^{2}.
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the polynomial $t$ can't be written as a linear combination of

$$
\{2,{t}^{2}\}
$$

since all these combinations result in polynomials without terms of the form $at.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-55e1e424-505b-5097-b514-ba9bc2cc90d9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-55e1e424-505b-5097-b514-ba9bc2cc90d9" :answer-field/id #uuid "55e1e424-505b-5097-b514-ba9bc2cc90d9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e75c2b7e-4724-50f4-baef-5d83a5a25436" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e75c2b7e-4724-50f4-baef-5d83a5a25436" "answer-18a10dfc-afa4-52d6-9bf7-b580f906a755" "answer-299a0ce7-32c9-5434-88c4-7d63337cd0bd" "answer-6e05ed0b-0f3c-5c51-9fcd-1cb42a9bc2e9" "answer-84245521-5afe-5940-8979-375abcac5604"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e75c2b7e-4724-50f4-baef-5d83a5a25436" :answer/id #uuid "e75c2b7e-4724-50f4-baef-5d83a5a25436" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-18a10dfc-afa4-52d6-9bf7-b580f906a755" :answer/id #uuid "18a10dfc-afa4-52d6-9bf7-b580f906a755" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-299a0ce7-32c9-5434-88c4-7d63337cd0bd" :answer/id #uuid "299a0ce7-32c9-5434-88c4-7d63337cd0bd" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6e05ed0b-0f3c-5c51-9fcd-1cb42a9bc2e9" :answer/id #uuid "6e05ed0b-0f3c-5c51-9fcd-1cb42a9bc2e9" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-84245521-5afe-5940-8979-375abcac5604" :answer/id #uuid "84245521-5afe-5940-8979-375abcac5604" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186360515 :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{3}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $3.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{1,t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${R}_{3}[t]$

II. ${t}^{3}-3t+8$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{1,t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}\}$

III. $\{1,t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}\}$ is a basis of ${R}_{3}[t]$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125245 :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}3 & 12 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186406882 :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 2 & -5\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186360523 :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186406881 :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]=2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-4)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of 

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}
$$

since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{21}=0:$

$$
a\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+b\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+c\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & c \\ 0 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-ac0d302b-9680-52bd-b447-e8dfc12a3304" :question/id #uuid "ac0d302b-9680-52bd-b447-e8dfc12a3304" :question/math-academy-id "q-107374" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Notice that

$$
1\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+0\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+0\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+0\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

where the first coefficient is nonzero, so the set is linearly dependent. In general, any set that contains a zero-matrix is linearly dependent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]=0\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+1\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-2)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+4\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the set is not linearly independent, it can't form a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1cfb4b04-4369-55b5-b86c-1bcf8c68a19d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1cfb4b04-4369-55b5-b86c-1bcf8c68a19d" :answer-field/id #uuid "1cfb4b04-4369-55b5-b86c-1bcf8c68a19d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-8a3f2158-ddfb-537c-810a-54533dd0a0c4" :answer-field/choices ["answer-bf2dcfe2-dcba-5af7-8a16-53d83c9d1420" "answer-8867cc1f-ad13-5b27-82c7-d9621d2bc854" "answer-6e6cbcc7-075a-5d4e-95fb-61a97ecac1f1" "answer-8a3f2158-ddfb-537c-810a-54533dd0a0c4" "answer-cd6d4c15-e447-5d3b-bdaf-eabf62f4dcbd"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bf2dcfe2-dcba-5af7-8a16-53d83c9d1420" :answer/id #uuid "bf2dcfe2-dcba-5af7-8a16-53d83c9d1420" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8867cc1f-ad13-5b27-82c7-d9621d2bc854" :answer/id #uuid "8867cc1f-ad13-5b27-82c7-d9621d2bc854" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6e6cbcc7-075a-5d4e-95fb-61a97ecac1f1" :answer/id #uuid "6e6cbcc7-075a-5d4e-95fb-61a97ecac1f1" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8a3f2158-ddfb-537c-810a-54533dd0a0c4" :answer/id #uuid "8a3f2158-ddfb-537c-810a-54533dd0a0c4" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cd6d4c15-e447-5d3b-bdaf-eabf62f4dcbd" :answer/id #uuid "cd6d4c15-e447-5d3b-bdaf-eabf62f4dcbd" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186244095 :question/problem "Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ and $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ be bases of ${R}^{3}$ and ${R}^{2}$, respectively. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$

II. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$

III. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$" :question/worked-solution "Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$, any vector of ${R}^{2},$ including the given vector $x,$ can be written as a linear combination of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ This means that $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x\}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

- Statement II is false. The set $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the vector ${b}_{3}$ is in ${R}^{3}$ but it is not a linear combination of  ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ as the set  $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. This means that the set does not span ${R}^{3}$ and therefore, cannot be a basis.

- Statement III is false. The set $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true"." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-2dd6c5c5-53ed-575f-8c9f-dc822f51b9e6" :question/id #uuid "2dd6c5c5-53ed-575f-8c9f-dc822f51b9e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-107537" :question/problem "Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}\}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$

II. $\{{b}_{1},2{b}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$

III. $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$" :question/worked-solution "Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. The set $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{2}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}(2{b}_{2}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+(2{x}_{2}){b}_{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\{{b}_{1},2{b}_{2}\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{{b}_{1},2{b}_{2}\}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}{b}_{2}
$$

- Statement III is false. The set $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the third vector is a linear combination of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ This means that the set is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f2baa79b-54b3-5737-acdd-b3964add504b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f2baa79b-54b3-5737-acdd-b3964add504b" :answer-field/id #uuid "f2baa79b-54b3-5737-acdd-b3964add504b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-013e97ca-b56e-5aee-9c9f-d304a8a1dbd7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1b5613e5-d85e-5aa4-87d6-6ad009986011" "answer-c794a74a-633c-5598-9aae-0206903fc293" "answer-4eb0c223-1e6e-53a8-9673-4bcd81bc316b" "answer-013e97ca-b56e-5aee-9c9f-d304a8a1dbd7" "answer-384b6eb0-e2bf-5f86-af7f-3398204e70e4"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1b5613e5-d85e-5aa4-87d6-6ad009986011" :answer/id #uuid "1b5613e5-d85e-5aa4-87d6-6ad009986011" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c794a74a-633c-5598-9aae-0206903fc293" :answer/id #uuid "c794a74a-633c-5598-9aae-0206903fc293" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4eb0c223-1e6e-53a8-9673-4bcd81bc316b" :answer/id #uuid "4eb0c223-1e6e-53a8-9673-4bcd81bc316b" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-013e97ca-b56e-5aee-9c9f-d304a8a1dbd7" :answer/id #uuid "013e97ca-b56e-5aee-9c9f-d304a8a1dbd7" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-384b6eb0-e2bf-5f86-af7f-3398204e70e4" :answer/id #uuid "384b6eb0-e2bf-5f86-af7f-3398204e70e4" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124862 :question/problem "Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}\}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},x\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$

II. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$

III. $\{{c}_{3},{c}_{2},{c}_{1}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$" :question/worked-solution "Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$, any vector of ${R}^{2},$ including the given vector $x,$ can be written as a linear combination of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}.$ This means that $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},x\}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

- Statement II is false. The set $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

- Statement III is true. The set $\{{c}_{3},{c}_{2},{c}_{1}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because, by reordering the vectors, we obtain the basis $C.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-c626f6f5-d2a8-58e2-a687-8abd5e7a0913" :question/id #uuid "c626f6f5-d2a8-58e2-a687-8abd5e7a0913" :question/math-academy-id "q-107941" :question/problem "Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\}$ is linearly dependent

II. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}\}$ is a basis for $V$

III. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{3},{b}_{1}+{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly dependent" :question/worked-solution "Since $B$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $B$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since if $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}({b}_{1}+{b}_{2})=0,
$$

where at least one of $x$'s is not zero. But then 

$$
({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+0{b}_{3}=0,
$$

which would mean that $B$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $B$ is a basis.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}(2{b}_{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+(2{x}_{3}){b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}\}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+\frac{{x}_{3}}{2}(2{b}_{3})
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the third vector is a linear combination of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4e2c51c7-77b4-56a2-ab4a-cf386667088e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-4e2c51c7-77b4-56a2-ab4a-cf386667088e" :answer-field/id #uuid "4e2c51c7-77b4-56a2-ab4a-cf386667088e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3bffe33d-8459-5da2-bb30-4e33f3a9a3a3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-6188c2a2-db52-5316-ac0b-78dce45a1839" "answer-3777d47d-2620-5df7-9137-5fe91751144e" "answer-68ec88dd-c105-5380-bc0a-502cd62f7812" "answer-3bffe33d-8459-5da2-bb30-4e33f3a9a3a3" "answer-bebe80cf-1236-5ad0-9caa-015b17550bea"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6188c2a2-db52-5316-ac0b-78dce45a1839" :answer/id #uuid "6188c2a2-db52-5316-ac0b-78dce45a1839" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3777d47d-2620-5df7-9137-5fe91751144e" :answer/id #uuid "3777d47d-2620-5df7-9137-5fe91751144e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-68ec88dd-c105-5380-bc0a-502cd62f7812" :answer/id #uuid "68ec88dd-c105-5380-bc0a-502cd62f7812" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3bffe33d-8459-5da2-bb30-4e33f3a9a3a3" :answer/id #uuid "3bffe33d-8459-5da2-bb30-4e33f3a9a3a3" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bebe80cf-1236-5ad0-9caa-015b17550bea" :answer/id #uuid "bebe80cf-1236-5ad0-9caa-015b17550bea" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186244093 :question/problem "Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}\}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$

II. $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$

III. $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{1}+{c}_{3}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$" :question/worked-solution "Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. The set $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the set contains a vector from another vector space.

- Statement II is false. The set $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{2}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{c}_{1}+{x}_{2}{c}_{2}+{x}_{3}({c}_{1}+{c}_{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}){c}_{1}+{x}_{2}{c}_{2}+{x}_{3}{c}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{1}+{c}_{3}\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $C$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{1}+{c}_{3}\}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{c}_{1}+{x}_{2}{c}_{2}+{x}_{3}{c}_{3}=({x}_{1}-{x}_{3}){c}_{1}+{x}_{2}{c}_{2}+{x}_{3}({c}_{1}+{c}_{3})
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125765 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbb{R}_n[t]$ denote the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $\mathbb{R}$ that have degree at most $n.$ Also, let $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ be the vector space of all $2 \times 2$ matrices over $\mathbb{R}.$ Then, we have the following important standard bases.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124490 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2dd6c5c5-53ed-575f-8c9f-dc822f51b9e6" "question-c626f6f5-d2a8-58e2-a687-8abd5e7a0913"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124303 :question/problem "Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}$ is a basis of $V$

II. $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}$ spans $V$

III. $\left\{  -\mathbf{b_2}, 3\mathbf{b_1}\right\}$ is linearly dependent" :question/worked-solution "Since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $\mathcal{B}$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $\mathcal{B}$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{2}+{x}_{2}(-{b}_{1})+{x}_{3}({b}_{3}+{b}_{1}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{2}+({x}_{3}-{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly independent, gives
![](images/62/625e812c25818cec68c6a5bcd59a39945feb09526607244e42059ed8af6f9b08.svg)
Also, $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3\mathbf{b}_3
=
x_2\mathbf{b}_2+(x_3-x_1)(-\mathbf{b}_1)+x_3 (\mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1})
$$

- Statement II is false. In order for $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}$ to span $V,$ every element of $\mathcal{B}$ must be able to be expressed as a linear combination of elements of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}.$ But the vector $\mathbf{b}_1 \in \mathcal{B}$ can't be written as a linear combination of the elements of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}.$

- Statement III is false. If $\left\{  -\mathbf{b_2}, 3\mathbf{b_1}\right\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist $x_1$ and $x_2$ not both zero such that

$$
x_1(-\mathbf{b_2}) + x_2(3\mathbf{b_1}) = \mathbf{0}.
$$

Then, we would have

$$
(3x_2) \cdot \mathbf{b_1} + (-x_1) \cdot \mathbf{b_2} + 0 \cdot \mathbf{b}_3= \mathbf{0}.
$$

But this would mean that $\mathcal{B} = \left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly dependent, which contradicts the fact that $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis of $V.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186360516 :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{3}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $3.$

III. $\{0,{t}^{3}\}$ is a basis of ${R}_{3}[t]$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186360514 :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{3}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $3.$

Which of the following statements are true?

III. $\{0,t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}\}$ is a basis of ${R}_{3}[t]$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186360513 :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{2}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $2.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{t,{t}^{2}\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${R}_{2}[t]$

II. ${t}^{2}+1$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{t,{t}^{2}\}$

III. $\{t,{t}^{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}_{2}[t]$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation 

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot t+{x}_{2}\cdot {t}^{2}=0,
$$

 
is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is false. Notice that all linear combinations of

$$
\{t,{t}^{2}\}
$$

result in polynomials without the constant term.

- Statement III is false. Indeed, the polynomial ${t}^{2}+1$ can't be written as a linear combination of the set  $\{t,{t}^{2}\}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-a024553e-c27e-5c68-a828-a6ec8223e683" :question/id #uuid "a024553e-c27e-5c68-a828-a6ec8223e683" :question/math-academy-id "q-107130" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{2}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $2.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{2,{t}^{2}\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${R}_{2}[t]$

II. $2+{t}^{2}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{2,{t}^{2}\}$

III. $\{2,{t}^{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}_{2}[t]$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation 

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot 2+{x}_{2}\cdot {t}^{2}=0,
$$

 
is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
2+{t}^{2}=1\cdot 2+1\cdot {t}^{2}.
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the polynomial $t$ can't be written as a linear combination of

$$
\{2,{t}^{2}\}

since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{21}=0:$

a\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+b\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+c\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & c \\ 0 & b\end{aligned}]

- Statement III is false. The set $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true"." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-2dd6c5c5-53ed-575f-8c9f-dc822f51b9e6" :question/id #uuid "2dd6c5c5-53ed-575f-8c9f-dc822f51b9e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-107537" :question/problem "Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}\}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively.

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

$$

$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\}$ is linearly dependent

II. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}\}$ is a basis for $V$

III. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{3},{b}_{1}+{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly dependent" :question/worked-solution "Since $B$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $B$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since if $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}({b}_{1}+{b}_{2})=0,
$$

where at least one of $x$'s is not zero. But then 

$$
({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+0{b}_{3}=0,
$$

which would mean that $B$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $B$ is a basis.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}(2{b}_{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+(2{x}_{3}){b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}\}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+\frac{{x}_{3}}{2}(2{b}_{3})

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{c}_{1}+{x}_{2}{c}_{2}+{x}_{3}({c}_{1}+{c}_{3}) & =0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}){c}_{1}+{x}_{2}{c}_{2}+{x}_{3}{c}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}

Which of the following statements are true?

II. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}\}$ is a basis for $V$

- $B$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $B$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since if $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}({b}_{1}+{b}_{2})=0,
$$

where at least one of $x$'s is not zero. But then 

$$
({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+0{b}_{3}=0,
$$

which would mean that $B$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $B$ is a basis.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}(2{b}_{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+(2{x}_{3}){b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}\}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+\frac{{x}_{3}}{2}(2{b}_{3})
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the third vector is a linear combination of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""] ["question-c626f6f5-d2a8-58e2-a687-8abd5e7a0913" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] $$

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 12 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]=0\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- $[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}$
- ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{4}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}={x}_{4}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}]=2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+8\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the set is linearly independent and for any matrix in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R),$ we get 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]=a\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+b\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+c\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+d\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} {:db/id 17592186406881 :question/id #uuid "455cce4b-aebd-5209-87a1-ec6ed81f2e6b" :question/math-academy-id "q-94867" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124489 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "073042ee-d96d-5872-9681-ddcea43a2d37" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About Sets of Vectors in a Matrix Vector Space"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "19ad696f-46c1-5b25-95e1-0f62a7d8c499" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186406853} {:answer/id #uuid "36961107-cd5d-5ec8-9558-b9c722111836" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186406854} {:answer/id #uuid "5b6d00a5-b721-58e6-9958-8240023a0a6b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186406859} {:answer/id #uuid "63e999ff-a2e3-5a48-9d48-fdfc510b1f5e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186406860} {:answer/id #uuid "fcaf053d-057d-585d-bf1a-9d33a99b8261" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186406873}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "19ad696f-46c1-5b25-95e1-0f62a7d8c499" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186406853} :answer-field/id #uuid "2bf21969-de75-57e4-b536-3fbad5aa15ae" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186406876}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- $[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}$
- ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]=2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-4)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of 

$$
{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}
$$

since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{21}=0:$

$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- $[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 2 & -5\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}$
- ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{4}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}={x}_{4}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 2 & -5\end{aligned}]=3\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-4)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-2)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-5)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the set is linearly independent and for any matrix in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R),$ we get 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]=a\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-b)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-c)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]+d\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} {:db/id 17592186124490 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124303 :question/id #uuid "91989c25-1d0d-5639-b3e1-7f7479322b7b" Vector Spaces"}] :question/problem "Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

- $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}$ is a basis of $V$

- $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}$ spans $V$

- $\left\{  -\mathbf{b_2}, 3\mathbf{b_1}\right\}$ is linearly dependent" :question/worked-solution "Since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $\mathcal{B}$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $\mathcal{B}$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{2}+{x}_{2}(-{b}_{1})+{x}_{3}({b}_{3}+{b}_{1}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{2}+({x}_{3}-{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly independent, gives
![](images/44/44e05962671a66862ed2fb7a4bc3fc2f859d3a66c56274b869724ee47f6c6414.png)
Also, $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3\mathbf{b}_3
=
x_2\mathbf{b}_2+(x_3-x_1)(-\mathbf{b}_1)+x_3 (\mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1})
$$

- Statement II is false. In order for $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}$ to span $V,$ every element of $\mathcal{B}$ must be able to be expressed as a linear combination of elements of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}.$ But the vector $\mathbf{b}_1 \in \mathcal{B}$ can't be written as a linear combination of the elements of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}.$

- Statement III is false. If $\left\{  -\mathbf{b_2}, 3\mathbf{b_1}\right\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist $x_1$ and $x_2$ not both zero such that

$$
x_1(-\mathbf{b_2}) + x_2(3\mathbf{b_1}) = \mathbf{0}.
$$

Then, we would have

$$
(3x_2) \cdot \mathbf{b_1} + (-x_1) \cdot \mathbf{b_2} + 0 \cdot \mathbf{b}_3= \mathbf{0}.
$$

But this would mean that $\mathcal{B} = \left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly dependent, which contradicts the fact that $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis of $V.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186124862 :question/id #uuid "6d5104d0-4e4f-5680-8c4e-7e5a0379f267" :question/math-academy-id "q-34638" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124490 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ca956d3e-37a8-5f0f-a062-97d0567d54e6" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About Bases of Abstract Vector Spaces"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b8b90d6-5674-5068-a2a2-4950704e8cb0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "None of the statements are true" :db/id 17592186317658} {:answer/id #uuid "86178245-9481-5f22-8d68-289af891d826" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186318021} {:answer/id #uuid "86d99d85-4d11-549a-b58b-bba5ef257d5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186318023} {:answer/id #uuid "9b6aaf84-f047-5e8e-ac8b-5719bdd7b98c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186318095} {:answer/id #uuid "a0bba391-5eca-543e-b163-e72fcd70aae1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186318115}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "86178245-9481-5f22-8d68-289af891d826" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186318021} :answer-field/id #uuid "30b03ae0-ed7b-5e49-9174-022c35181d38" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186318521}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively.

- ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3},w}$ is linearly independent
- ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ is linearly dependent
- ${{b}_{1},3{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}}$ is a basis of $V$" :question/worked-solution "Since $B$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $B$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $B$ is a basis of $V,$ it is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors. This means that if we add any new vector to the set, it becomes linearly dependent.

- Statement II is false. Since if ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ is linearly dependent then there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}=0,
$$

where at least one of $x$'s is not zero. But then 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+0{b}_{3}=0,
$$

which would mean that $B$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $B$ is a basis.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}(3{b}_{2})+{x}_{3}(2{b}_{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+(3{x}_{2}){b}_{2}+(2{x}_{3}){b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ 3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, ${{b}_{1},3{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${{b}_{1},3{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+\frac{{x}_{2}}{3}(3{b}_{2})+\frac{{x}_{3}}{2}(2{b}_{3})
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""} {:db/id 17592186406883 :question/id #uuid "b3557614-de80-516a-bb07-7b50ae99a56a" :question/math-academy-id "q-80631" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4a4b0b94-d6cc-5fc8-aaef-54da3f8e617b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186406856} {:answer/id #uuid "74ca9113-b90b-5028-9c16-d6040c62cabf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186406862} {:answer/id #uuid "9276fe19-6956-5810-a884-2421c6c56cc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186406863} {:answer/id #uuid "b1f78152-7f85-5618-be57-9777140dfe2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186406865} {:answer/id #uuid "e4af5006-271e-5598-b528-2bbabe13d95d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186406872}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406872} :answer-field/id #uuid "c77beab8-8132-549d-89ed-5a3840170386" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186406878}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ are bases of ${R}^{3}$ and ${R}^{2}$, respectively. 

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${x,{b}_{2},{c}_{1}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$
- ${-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$
- ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. The set ${x,{b}_{2},{c}_{1}}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(-2{b}_{3})+{x}_{2}(3{b}_{1})+{x}_{3}(5{b}_{2}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2{x}_{1}){b}_{3}+(3{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+(5{x}_{3}){b}_{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}=0 \\ 3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, ${-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}(3{b}_{1})+\frac{{x}_{2}}{5}(5{b}_{2})+(-\frac{{x}_{3}}{2})(-2{b}_{3})
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$, any vector of ${R}^{2},$ including the given vector $x,$ can be written as a linear combination of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ This means that ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} {:db/id 17592186124592 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124403 :question/id #uuid "92adb651-e2db-5296-817d-aea249afe2b4" :question/math-academy-id "e-8269"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2588e089-4786-5346-b42d-65c2740ae2ab" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048257}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124966 :question/id #uuid "96532d4b-53ae-5b0b-a44e-d0ba6b721786" :question/math-academy-id "q-36308"} {:db/id 17592186125244 :question/id #uuid "7a80ea94-714a-5496-91f4-d59c30bb26ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-94851"} {:db/id 17592186244029 :question/id #uuid "38344b2a-4c7e-5844-831c-94e852b34e5a" :question/math-academy-id "q-107131"} {:db/id 17592186360513 :question/id #uuid "ac8aaff6-9636-552f-aae2-acac5b76a9ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-94842"} {:db/id 17592186360514 :question/id #uuid "d8792da5-8116-548d-a9e9-a07944635528" :question/math-academy-id "q-94847"} {:db/id 17592186360515 :question/id #uuid "b873442b-9d2d-5d41-a7b6-d67882fe4b7f" :question/math-academy-id "q-94848"} {:db/id 17592186360516 :question/id #uuid "bf9e33e0-00b4-5d7d-a1a7-55573563c2a8" :question/math-academy-id "q-94850"}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About Sets of Vectors in a Polynomial Vector Space"} {:db/id 17592186124403 :question/id #uuid "92adb651-e2db-5296-817d-aea249afe2b4" :question/math-academy-id "e-8269" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186124592 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2588e089-4786-5346-b42d-65c2740ae2ab" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About Sets of Vectors in a Polynomial Vector Space"}] :question/problem "Consider the vector space $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $\mathbb R$ with degrees at most $2.$

- ${t}^{3}-3t+8$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${1,t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}}$

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125350 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125763 :tutorial/content "A set of vectors 

$$
\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n \}
$$

is called a **basis** of an abstract vector space $V$ if the following two conditions hold:

- $\mathcal{B}$ is linearly independent, and

- $\mathcal{B}$ spans $V.$

For example, let's consider the vector space $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $\mathbb R$ with degree at most $2,$ and its subset 

$$
\mathcal{B} = \left\{ {\color{blue}{1}}, {\color{blue}{t}}, {\color{blue}{t^2}} \right\}.
$$

 

Is $\mathcal{B}$ a basis for $\mathbb{R}_2[t]?$ Let's check our two conditions.

- First, we check for linear independence. Notice that the equation 

$$
x_1 \cdot {\color{blue}1} + x_2 \cdot {\color{blue}t} + x_3 \cdot {\color{blue}t^2} = 0
$$

 
is true for all $t$ if and only if 

$$
x_1=x_2=x_3=0.
$$

Therefore, the set $\mathcal{B}$ is linearly independent in $\mathbb{R}_2[t].$

- Next, we check that $\mathcal B$ spans $\mathbb{R}_2[t].$ Notice that we can write any polynomial $at^2+bt+c\in\mathbb{R}_2[t]$ as a linear combination of vectors from $\mathcal{B} \mathbin{:}$

$$
at^2+bt+c=c\cdot{\color{blue}1} + b\cdot{\color{blue}t} + a\cdot{\color{blue}t^2}
$$

Therefore, $\mathcal B$ spans $\mathbb{R}_2[t].$

Since both conditions hold, we conclude that $\mathcal{B} = \{ {1}, {t}, {t^2} \}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$." :tutorial/id #uuid "1d94c7bd-3777-5331-b633-0e2463092e26" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3210 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b18f66cf-141c-5d9b-abc4-5dec05218f63" :step/math-academy-id 17522 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125527}} {:db/id 17592186125351 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124489 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124302 :question/id #uuid "4b1227cb-7cf9-534d-a22f-e7acf7df9dc9" :question/math-academy-id "e-4830"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "073042ee-d96d-5872-9681-ddcea43a2d37" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125002} {:db/id 17592186125245} {:db/id 17592186244046} {:db/id 17592186244069} {:db/id 17592186244070} {:db/id 17592186360519} {:db/id 17592186360520} {:db/id 17592186360521} {:db/id 17592186360522} {:db/id 17592186360523} {:db/id 17592186406881} {:db/id 17592186406882}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About Sets of Vectors in a Matrix Vector Space"} :step/id #uuid "c37255e8-78c3-5483-a38d-706de2e319e3" :step/math-academy-id 17523 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125352}} {:db/id 17592186125352 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125764 :tutorial/content "A set of vectors $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ is a basis of a vector space $V$ if $\mathcal{B}$ is a **maximally linearly independent set in $V$**. In other words, $\mathcal{B}$ is linearly independent and for any vector ${\color{blue}\mathbf{w}} \in V,$ the set

- The standard basis of $\mathbb{R}_n[t]$ is $\{ 1, \: t, \: \ldots, \: t^n \}.$

- The standard basis of $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${x,{b}_{2},{c}_{1}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$
- ${-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$
- ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. The set ${x,{b}_{2},{c}_{1}}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(-2{b}_{3})+{x}_{2}(3{b}_{1})+{x}_{3}(5{b}_{2}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2{x}_{1}){b}_{3}+(3{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+(5{x}_{3}){b}_{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}=0 \\ 3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, ${-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}(3{b}_{1})+\frac{{x}_{2}}{5}(5{b}_{2})+(-\frac{{x}_{3}}{2})(-2{b}_{3})
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$, any vector of ${R}^{2},$ including the given vector $x,$ can be written as a linear combination of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ This means that ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} :step/id #uuid "748c2276-dafd-5926-8dff-6ce428e10c5e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406887}} {:db/id 17592186406885 :step/content {:db/id 17592186406880 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "04483552-efe7-5ac0-9f49-b7cb22e5f5db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186406850} {:answer/id #uuid "154ae220-9109-5b3d-9009-7a90d7f05763" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186406852} {:answer/id #uuid "67110d56-fa92-5c33-8463-9dec2842fc83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186406861} {:answer/id #uuid "d33ae3a1-a6f3-5f6a-a11e-e64513528243" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186406869} {:answer/id #uuid "e179725d-36ab-557d-b57d-805d29bd2ec6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186406870}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406861} :answer-field/id #uuid "21abb11f-a753-536d-8ed2-e4d2105529ba" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186406875}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "1d66ed66-f11f-53c8-af0e-1883d2bbdd40" :question/math-academy-id "q-94942" :question/problem "Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3},w}$ is linearly independent
- ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ is linearly dependent
- ${{b}_{1},3{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}}$ is a basis of $V$" :question/worked-solution "Since $B$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $B$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $B$ is a basis of $V,$ it is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors. This means that if we add any new vector to the set, it becomes linearly dependent.

- Statement II is false. Since if ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ is linearly dependent then there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}=0,
$$

where at least one of $x$'s is not zero. But then 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+0{b}_{3}=0,
$$

which would mean that $B$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $B$ is a basis.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}(3{b}_{2})+{x}_{3}(2{b}_{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+(3{x}_{2}){b}_{2}+(2{x}_{3}){b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ 3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, ${{b}_{1},3{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${{b}_{1},3{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+\frac{{x}_{2}}{3}(3{b}_{2})+\frac{{x}_{3}}{2}(2{b}_{3})
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""} :step/id #uuid "aa1dd52d-ebd7-598e-b1e9-f1f6411b6354" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406888}} {:db/id 17592186406886 :step/content {:db/id 17592186406881 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "19ad696f-46c1-5b25-95e1-0f62a7d8c499" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186406853} {:answer/id #uuid "36961107-cd5d-5ec8-9558-b9c722111836" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186406854} {:answer/id #uuid "5b6d00a5-b721-58e6-9958-8240023a0a6b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186406859} {:answer/id #uuid "63e999ff-a2e3-5a48-9d48-fdfc510b1f5e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186406860} {:answer/id #uuid "fcaf053d-057d-585d-bf1a-9d33a99b8261" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186406873}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406853} :answer-field/id #uuid "2bf21969-de75-57e4-b536-3fbad5aa15ae" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186406876}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "455cce4b-aebd-5209-87a1-ec6ed81f2e6b" :question/math-academy-id "q-94867" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- $[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}$
- ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]=2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-4)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of 

$$
{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}
$$

since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{21}=0:$

$$
a\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+b\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+c\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & c \\ 0 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} :step/id #uuid "bc7cf94a-8206-5fe0-b854-5c6affbe827a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406885}} {:db/id 17592186406887 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125245 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4dc69c43-a9f7-5f43-890e-96fe06c46748" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186406857} {:answer/id #uuid "5129302f-a0d3-5c48-9cd2-710367d9ef9b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186406858} {:answer/id #uuid "ba2afd25-1b47-58bd-a63a-fb16ca010eec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186406866} {:answer/id #uuid "e47c35f7-6343-5a83-8c29-d0f93c6a25ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186406871} {:answer/id #uuid "fecfaf5f-f070-5827-a2e0-854b742a089f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186406874}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406866} :answer-field/id #uuid "9a0b26bf-4452-55f8-96b7-34adf0df266d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186406877}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cceedad6-c377-5d6a-a68c-beab3237c2c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-94866" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- $[\begin{aligned}3 & 12 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}$
- ${[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Notice that

$$
1\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+0\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

where the first coefficient is nonzero, so the set is linearly dependent. In general, any set that contains a zero-matrix is linearly dependent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 12 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]=0\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the set is not linearly independent, it can't form a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} :step/id #uuid "d8519c82-2015-5d4b-ab7d-68f0931d52be" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406886}} {:db/id 17592186406888 :step/content {:db/id 17592186406882 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10d895ea-b8fa-5d9f-8273-d0bb03153342" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186406851} {:answer/id #uuid "46e97098-e4a4-5102-a43d-56b2c717a39c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186406855} {:answer/id #uuid "96a48ad5-c7b2-53c5-9bdb-aa723c9b9fc4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186406864} {:answer/id #uuid "be96ccd4-bd92-5133-aad2-a91841ec919a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186406867} {:answer/id #uuid "c6fdb3c3-35ae-5bf6-800c-8390e5189040" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186406868}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406867} :answer-field/id #uuid "dc08e474-6dee-51de-a67a-78ce180dd388" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186406879}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5b0d7b89-c3c8-5cee-b6a2-01b5cd1b1f67" :question/math-academy-id "q-107533" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 2 & -5\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}$
- ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

$$

$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}={x}_{4}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the set is linearly independent and for any matrix in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R),$ we get 

$$

$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} :step/id #uuid "f5d3d190-875f-5a88-afc2-f8fcfd0bc6a4"}] :activity/title "Bases in Abstract Vector Spaces" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186406849} {:db/id 17592186046673} {:db/id 17592186406884 :step/content {:db/id 17592186406883 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4a4b0b94-d6cc-5fc8-aaef-54da3f8e617b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186406856} {:answer/id #uuid "74ca9113-b90b-5028-9c16-d6040c62cabf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186406862} {:answer/id #uuid "9276fe19-6956-5810-a884-2421c6c56cc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186406863} {:answer/id #uuid "b1f78152-7f85-5618-be57-9777140dfe2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186406865} {:answer/id #uuid "e4af5006-271e-5598-b528-2bbabe13d95d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186406872}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406872} :answer-field/id #uuid "c77beab8-8132-549d-89ed-5a3840170386" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186406878}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b3557614-de80-516a-bb07-7b50ae99a56a" :question/math-academy-id "q-80631" :question/problem "Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ are bases of ${R}^{3}$ and ${R}^{2}$, respectively.

where at least one of $x$'s is not zero. But then 

$$

which would mean that $B$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $B$ is a basis.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}(3{b}_{2})+{x}_{3}(2{b}_{3}) & =0\end{aligned}

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+(3{x}_{2}){b}_{2}+(2{x}_{3}){b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}

which, since ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
